title: Platform infrastructure
subtitle: From an empty Databricks account to a student's first deploy
notes: Every lecture so far started inside a workspace that already existed. Today we look underneath: what Databricks is made of, how the course's account, identities, catalogs, GitHub and onboarding were built, and why all of it is code.

title: Agenda
rows: Cloud provider, control plane, compute plane, storage
Admin roles, principals, groups, the one-time setup
The daily run, and the move of 2 November

title: Your Databricks account, and your cloud account
grid: Web application, REST APIs, jobs, **Unity Catalog**, small notebook results
Nothing: the control plane is always Databricks'
**Serverless**: notebooks, jobs, SQL warehouses, model serving, apps. The course uses only this
**Classic**: clusters in your VPC, no public IPs, connecting out to the control plane
**Default storage** of a serverless workspace: tables, volumes, the workspace's own files
Your S3 bucket: workspace storage of a classic workspace, external data
cloud: Two separate perimeters, as in Databricks' architecture picture; users and applications come in from outside. The course: express setup, a serverless workspace on AWS `us-west-2`, so everything is in your Databricks account and you have no cloud account.
notes: The control plane is Databricks' backend: the web application and the services behind it, run by Databricks in your Databricks account, outside your cloud account. The compute plane is where data is processed. Serverless compute runs in Databricks' account, in the same region; classic compute runs in the customer's account and connects out through secure cluster connectivity, with no open ports and no public IPs. A serverless workspace, which is what express setup gives you, uses only serverless compute and default storage. Traffic between the control plane and serverless compute stays on the cloud backbone. To show Databricks' own picture, open the architecture diagram on the high-level architecture page (first source) live.

title: One query, end to end
rows: Browser or laptop sends the query to the **control plane**, signed in as you
Routes it to your warehouse in the **compute plane**
Checks your privileges on catalog, schema and table; audits the access
The driver splits the work; executors read the files **in parallel**
Small: back through the control plane. Large: files you download from storage
bottom: The interactive page lets you step through this for a notebook cell, a laptop query and a CD job.
notes: Hop 3 is a simplification: the docs describe Unity Catalog's privilege checks and auditing, but not exactly how Databricks' own compute receives its short-lived access to the files. Say so if asked.

title: Results come home two ways
rows: Notebook results that are small stay in the control plane and are shown in your browser.
Larger notebook results, and every job's results, are written to the workspace storage.
Above 1 MB, a SQL client gets presigned URLs and downloads Arrow files straight from storage, in parallel.
bottom: Where results live matters for governance: in a classic workspace that storage is a bucket in **your** account.
notes: Cloud Fetch applies to query results larger than 1 MB; files are up to 20 MB each and are cleaned up after about two days. The Python SQL connector uses Cloud Fetch by default and needs PyArrow.

title: Four admin roles, four scopes
table: Workspaces, metastores, users, service principals, account groups, federation policies. Only account admins create workspaces
One workspace: entitlements, compute, warehouses, `CAN MANAGE` on every object
Every Unity Catalog securable: grants and ownership. Optional, highly privileged
bottom: Give roles and ownership to **groups**: the course's metastore is owned by `grp-owners-llmops`, the teachers.
notes: The course found that creating a usage policy through the account API needed the billing admin role; account admin alone was refused at the first rehearsal.

title: Users, service principals and groups
table: What it does in the course
The daily onboarding: account, billing and workspace admin
Deploys the monitoring bundle; a user with grants, not an admin
Assessment evals on pull requests; in no group, five grants
Three per student: deploy your bundle to one environment each
owners, admins, students, teachers, services: every grant goes to one
bottom: Workspace-local groups are legacy: no Unity Catalog grants. Entitlements are explicit since 14 September 2026.
notes: Since 14 September 2026 the users group carries no entitlement; principals get workspace-access, databricks-sql-access or workspace-consume explicitly. A deploy principal without one was refused by the workspace APIs in the course's first rehearsal. In a company, an identity provider such as Entra ID or Okta usually owns users and groups through automatic identity management or SCIM.

title: The one-time setup is a script, not clicks
code:
# course-assistant: read first, the default is a dry run
PYTHONPATH=src uv run python scripts/setup_cohort.py \
    --profile course-account

# write, then dry-run again: every part says "exists"
PYTHONPATH=src uv run python scripts/setup_cohort.py \
    --profile course-account --apply

# parts, in dependency order
principals  account-admin  billing-admin  groups
owners  metastore  system-schemas  warehouse
catalog  catalogs  secret  destinations  budget
lakebase  evals  teachers  ...
rows: Some objects must exist before any automation can run: its own identity, roles, groups, catalogs.
Every part looks up by name before it creates; the default only reads.
The profile is always named, and refused if it points at another account.
notes: Run by an account admin from a laptop with an OAuth profile. The order matters: the groups before the metastore hand-over, the metastore before any grant on system, the warehouse before the catalog part whose SQL runs on it.

title: Your schema, in three catalogs
table: You: `ALL PRIVILEGES` and `MANAGE`. Your dev principal: `ALL PRIVILEGES`
You: read only. That environment's principal: `ALL PRIVILEGES`
Owned by `grp-admins-llmops`; `USE CATALOG` to the students group
The course's tables, secrets, model services; you reach `gateway` and your own rows
bottom: Privileges are inherited downwards; reading a table also needs `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`.
notes: Demo p2_unity_catalog_tour.py shows each privilege with where it is inherited from. Workspace-catalog binding (ISOLATED) is the usual way to make a production catalog reachable only from the production workspace.

title: One workspace, many tenants
rows: `pol-llmops-<you>` tags your serverless usage, so billing attributes it to you
`wh-llmops-<you>`, 2X-Small, stopped when made; tagged, since policies skip warehouses
`/llmops/<you>`, with its traces in your dev schema
`<type>-<purpose>-<owner>`: a deterministic name is how code finds an object again
notes: A non-admin cannot create a SQL warehouse, but can create a Lakebase project or a vector search endpoint; those bill while they exist, so a guard job deletes unregistered ones.

title: A workflow becomes a service principal
rows: The federation policy of `sp-deploy-<you>-prd`: issuer, subject, audience
Databricks returns an OAuth token for that principal
`databricks bundle deploy -t prd` runs as the principal
bottom: `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` is not a secret. One principal per environment: a dev token can never deploy to prd.
notes: Repositories created after 15 July 2026 send immutable subjects with the owner and repository ids, so a re-created or forked repository does not inherit the trust, and a policy with names only does not match. Databricks recommends the environment form of the subject. Demo: .github/workflows/whoami.yml prints the claims and the identity.

title: How automation should sign in
table: Recommended: CI/CD and any platform that issues tokens. No Databricks secret
Unattended jobs where federation is impossible. Secrets: at most 730 days, deleted after 90 days unused
You on your laptop: `databricks auth login`
Legacy: one workspace, one person's rights
bottom: All of them share **unified authentication**: arguments, then environment variables, then `~/.databrickscfg`.

title: Give every automation its own narrow identity
table: Onboarding, monitoring, evals and each student's deploys: separate service principals, never a person
`sp-deploy-<you>-dev` writes dev only; a leaked dev token cannot touch prd
Admin only where the API demands it
Only `sp-onboarding-llmops` is admin: creating users and usage policies needs it
Every workflow signs in by OIDC; the one stored secret is the GitHub App key
`system.access.audit` records every call, every secret read
bottom: A deploy pipeline is the most powerful user on the platform, and nobody watches it type.
notes: Contrast with a PAT in a CI variable: one person's rights in every environment until it expires or they leave; rotation by hand; a leak invisible until used. OAuth secrets are better scoped but still stored, and since 16 September 2026 an unused one is deleted after 90 days.

title: Three places for a secret
table: One workspace; ACL per scope (READ, WRITE, MANAGE): who reads one secret reads all. 1,000 scopes, 128 KB a value
Azure only; a read-only window on a vault you manage in Azure. Access policies, not RBAC; the scope exposes the whole vault
`catalog.schema.secret` in every workspace on the metastore; `READ SECRET` per secret; reads audited; 60 KiB
bottom: On AWS and Azure a Unity Catalog schema can also front AWS Secrets Manager or Key Vault (Beta).
notes: Creating a scope: databricks secrets create-scope; reading: dbutils.secrets.get(scope=, key=), redacted in output. UC: databricks secrets-uc create-secret, dbutils.secrets.get(catalog=, schema=, key=). The course keeps its few secrets in course_ops.secrets.

title: Where each kind of secret reaches
rows: `{{secrets/scope/key}}` in compute environment variables, model serving environment variables and Databricks Apps resources
Read in code: `dbutils` in notebooks and jobs (environment 4+), the SDK in an app, a UDF's SECRETS clause
The app reads its credentials with `w.secrets_uc.get_secret`, because an app resource cannot name a UC secret
bottom: Choose by who must read it and where: governance favours Unity Catalog, configuration references still need scopes.
notes: Lecture 5's change: the App was given UC secrets and reads them in code; the alternative is a scope referenced as an app resource. Better still for an app: its own service principal with granted resources and no secret at all, or on-behalf-of-user auth.

title: Five ways to make the same volume
table: Strength, and what you still own
The fallback when no SDK fits: you write paging, retries, errors
Typed calls, retries, unified auth. Imperative: you decide what should exist
One command per call; shell and CI. No state
Declarative project resources with targets; the recommended CI/CD path. Terraform engine removed in CLI 1.20
Declarative with a plan; cloud and account level. You keep the state file
bottom: Run each twice: the second run is where they differ. Demo: `notebooks/platform/four_ways/`.

title: The ensure pattern makes imperative code safe
rows: The deterministic name is the key; no state file to lose.
created, adopted, updated: the run's audit trail.
notes: This is the shape of every onboarding step in course-assistant. The SDK is used there because the run loops over a student list from a sheet, calls GitHub in the same run, and records each step in a table: the list is the desired state, the audit table is the state.

title: Live: onboard one student by hand, three ways
rows: `plan` → `apply` → `plan` says No changes → `destroy`. Two providers, a state file
`create` → `show` → `delete`. Typed calls; run create twice and it fails
The same calls with URLs and JSON by hand; only the sign-in is borrowed
Add the row to the sheet; `onboarding.yml` with `only=` makes all of it, and much more
bottom: User, usage policy, schema and warehouse: the onboarding's first four Databricks steps, with the same names.
notes: Runbook: notebooks/platform/onboard_by_hand/README.md. Leave a minute or two between one tool's delete and the next tool's create: identity changes take that long to settle everywhere.

title: How course-assistant is set up
notes: Three automated parts share one state, the course_ops tables: the daily onboarding run (GitHub Actions as sp-onboarding-llmops) provisions each student and renders their repository; the student's repository deploys their own bundle as their own principals; the monitoring bundle reads the system tables for the teachers' dashboard and Genie agent. Every workflow signs in by OIDC. Source: course-assistant docs/figures/system-overview.html.
rows: GitHub Actions, daily, as `sp-onboarding-llmops`: provisions each student, renders their repository
Deploys the student's own bundle as their own principal per environment
Reads system tables for the teachers' dashboard and Genie agent
The `course_ops` tables; every workflow signs in by OIDC

title: One daily run, every step idempotent
rows: The sheet: email, GitHub, Discord, plan
user, policy, catalog, warehouse, experiment, repo, principals, invitations, first deploys, Lakebase
Job summary and a Teams card
bottom: A failed step holds only the steps that need it; a student who leaves is reported first, removed later.
notes: Runs once a day from GitHub Actions as sp-onboarding-llmops, signed in by OIDC from main of course-assistant. The repo step waits for the warehouse and policy ids because a repository is rendered once.

title: 2 November 2026
table: Compute blocked after a payment-method update: every query and model call refused
The API answers "Workspace … has been banned"
A new express setup workspace in a second account; the repository points at it
Setup script, cohort tables, GitHub variables; onboarding in narrowing runs: teachers' projects, a dry run, one test student, everyone
bottom: Student repositories survived: they live in GitHub. The onboarding gave them new principals and variables.
notes: What did not come back was data no code makes: tables and traces written in the old workspace, which no compute could read while it was blocked. Runbook: course-assistant docs/RUNBOOK.md, A new workspace.

title: What comes back, and what does not
rows: Users, schemas, grants, warehouses, principals, jobs, apps: rebuilt by running the code again
Tables a pipeline writes: rebuilt by re-running it, if the source still exists
Uncommitted notebooks, clicked objects, traces: gone. That is what backups are for
bottom: Databricks' DR guidance: treat every workspace artifact as infrastructure as code. There is no one-click move.
notes: The Terraform exporter can capture an existing workspace's configuration but is experimental, and does not cover MLflow data or secrets. Demo: inventory.py lists what you own and what your bundle declares.

title: Homework
rows: Run `p2_unity_catalog_tour.py`; explain each privilege on your acc schema and where it comes from
Run `inventory.py`; move one hand-made object into your bundle and deploy it
Make the volume two ways from `four_ways/`, run each twice, compare, then delete
Copy `whoami.yml` into your repository, use `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID_DEV`, run it, and match the subject to your dev principal
